screens.title: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn what a Virtual Private Cloud is and why it matters for secure architecture on AWS. A VPC is your private slice of the cloud where you control IP ranges, subnets, route tables, and gateways. Think of it like designing an office building: floors and rooms map to subnets and availability zones, and doors map to gateways and routes. You will see how CIDR notation determines how many addresses you get, how subnets group resources by function and availability zone, and why public and private subnets affect whether resources are reachable from the internet. We will walk through the practical steps to create a VPC, attach an Internet Gateway, set up route tables, and launch an EC2 instance that can serve traffic. Along the way you’ll learn common pitfalls — for example, assigning a route without a public IP will still leave an instance unreachable. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a basic, production-ready VPC with clear reasoning about addressing, isolation, and internet access. Keep the reservation rules and AZ boundaries in mind as you build — they often explain unexpected behavior.

screens.title: Skills You Will Practice
screens.narratorSegment: This page expands the practical skills you will use. You will practice choosing a VPC CIDR that avoids overlap with existing networks so you can peer or build VPNs later. For example, choosing 10.0.0.0/16 gives many addresses, but using 10.0.1.0/24 for a public subnet reserves a small, predictable pool for internet-facing services. You will also associate route tables correctly so that subnets intended to be public have a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway. In practice, a common mistake is creating the route but forgetting to associate it with the subnet, which leaves instances unreachable. You will configure EC2 launch options to auto-assign public IPs or attach Elastic IPs so web servers can be reached. Finally, you will reason about availability zones: each subnet is tied to a single AZ, so high availability requires at least one public and one private subnet in two different AZs. These are the operational skills exam scenarios and production deployments expect you to demonstrate.

screens.title: What is an Amazon VPC?
screens.narratorSegment: A Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, is an isolated virtual network inside AWS where you launch resources under your control. Put simply, it gives you address space, segmentation, and routing the way you would design an on-prem network, but as configurable cloud infrastructure. The VPC's address space is defined with CIDR notation; for example, 10.0.0.0/16 sets the range for the whole VPC. Once defined, you subdivide that space into subnets that live in single Availability Zones. This isolation matters because it separates your workloads from others in the shared AWS environment and lets you enforce precise security and routing rules. A concrete example: you might create a VPC with 10.0.0.0/16, then make a public subnet 10.0.1.0/24 for web servers and a private subnet 10.0.2.0/24 for databases. A common misconception is to assume the VPC alone grants internet access; it does not. An Internet Gateway and the right route configuration are required for internet connectivity. Takeaway: treat the VPC as your network design boundary — plan CIDR, subnets, and AZ mapping before provisioning instances. What is an Amazon VPC? means a vpc is your isolated, configurable network space in aws where you control addressing and connectivity.. In practical terms, an isolated virtual network you design and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A VPC is your isolated, configurable network space in AWS where you control addressing and connectivity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a VPC?
VPC explained
An isolated virtual network that you define: address block, subnets per AZ, route tables, and gateways.
Analogy
Designing an office building: floors and rooms are subnets; doors are gateways; corridors are routes.
Concrete example
VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with public subnet 10.0.1.0/24 for web, private subnet 10.0.2.0/24 for DB in the same region.
Key Takeaway

The VPC is the design boundary for your network. Plan CIDR and subnets first, then attach gateways and routes.

Important notes
  • Every AWS account gets a default VPC per region, but custom VPCs are needed for production control.
  • Subnets must reside entirely within one Availability Zone.
  • VPC does not imply internet access — IGW and routing are required.
  • Avoid CIDR overlap with on-premises networks or other VPCs you plan to peer with.
Common misconception
Attaching a VPC to the cloud does not automatically allow outbound internet traffic. You need an IGW and correct routing, plus public IPs on instances.

screens.title: Designing a VPC: CIDR → Subnets → AZs
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a VPC is a small process with lasting consequences. First, pick a CIDR block for the entire VPC, such as 10.0.0.0/16. This choice defines your total address capacity and must avoid overlap with on-premise or peered VPCs. Second, subdivide the CIDR into subnets aligned to availability zones. For example, split 10.0.0.0/16 into multiple /24 subnets like 10.0.1.0/24 in us-east-1a and 10.0.2.0/24 in us-east-1b. Each subnet belongs to a single AZ; that mapping is the central principle for high availability. Third, classify each subnet as public or private based on whether it will have a route to an Internet Gateway. Public subnets host internet-facing resources; private subnets host internal services like databases. Fourth, plan route tables and associations so intended destinations match the subnet's role. A common error is creating a public route but failing to associate the route table with the subnet, leaving instances with no outbound path. Example: create a public route table with 0.0.0.0/0 -> IGW and associate it to 10.0.1.0/24. Takeaway: design first, then implement, and verify associations and public IP assignments. Designing a VPC: CIDR → Subnets → AZs means choose cidr, carve subnets per az, classify public vs private, and configure routes before launching resources.. In practical terms, a step-by-step design process for a resilient network. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design steps
keyIdea.text: Choose CIDR, carve subnets per AZ, classify public vs private, and configure routes before launching resources.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Designing a VPC
CIDR to Subnets: four-step process
1. Pick CIDR
Example: choose 10.0.0.0/16 to give 65,536 addresses for growth.
2. Carve subnets per AZ
Make predictable blocks like 10.0.1.0/24 in AZ A, 10.0.2.0/24 in AZ B.
3. Classify public/private
Public subnets need a route to an IGW; private ones should not have that route.
4. Plan route tables
Define route rules, associate them with the right subnets, and verify with a test instance.
Example scenario
Design an app with web servers in 10.0.1.0/24 public subnets across two AZs and databases in 10.0.2.0/24 private subnets across two AZs for redundancy.
Key Takeaway

Map subnets to AZs deliberately; that mapping is the foundation of high availability.

screens.title: Hands-on CLI: Build a VPC and Public Subnet
screens.narratorSegment: We'll step through the CLI commands used to build a simple VPC with a public subnet. This walkthrough ties the abstract design to concrete commands and helps you spot the important outputs to record. First, you create the VPC with a CIDR such as 10.0.0.0/16 and note the VpcId. Next, create a subnet in a specific availability zone with a /24 like 10.0.1.0/24 and keep the SubnetId. Then create an Internet Gateway and attach it to the VPC; attach operations must reference both the VpcId and the InternetGatewayId. Create a route table for the VPC, add a route for 0.0.0.0/0 targeting the IGW, and associate the route table with the subnet. A practical mistake to avoid is skipping the associate step or forgetting to enable auto-assign public IP at instance launch. As an example, the aws ec2 create-vpc command returns the VpcId; use that value in subsequent calls. After this sequence you can launch an EC2 into the subnet, ensuring the public IP is assigned. Final takeaway: the sequence matters and recording the returned resource IDs is essential to connect steps.

keyIdea.title: CLI sequence
keyIdea.text: Create VPC → create subnet → create & attach IGW → create route table & route → associate route table with subnet.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CLI: Build a VPC
Command sequence
Create VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyCustomVPC}]'
# Note the VpcId in the output
Create subnet
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyPublicSubnet}]'
# Note the SubnetId
Internet Gateway
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=internet-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyVPC-IGW}]'
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --internet-gateway-id <YourInternetGatewayId>
Route table
aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id <YourVpcId>
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <YourRouteTableId> --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id <YourInternetGatewayId>
aws ec2 associate-route-table --subnet-id <YourSubnetId> --route-table-id <YourRouteTableId>
Common mistake
Forgetting to associate the route table with the subnet or forgetting to enable auto-assign public IP will prevent internet connectivity even if the route exists.

screens.title: CIDR Blocks and IP Allocation
screens.narratorSegment: CIDR notation is the mechanism AWS uses to assign address ranges to VPCs and subnets. It combines a base IP and a prefix length that defines how many bits are fixed, and therefore how many addresses are available. For instance, 10.0.0.0/16 reserves the first 16 bits and yields 2 to the power of 16 addresses, which is 65,536. Subnets use smaller CIDR blocks, like /24, which provides 256 addresses. In AWS, there are additional constraints: the platform reserves the first four and the last IP address in each subnet for internal use. That means in a 10.0.0.0/24 subnet addresses like 10.0.0.0 and 10.0.0.255 are not usable for your instances, plus a few others within the first four. A concrete example: a /24 subnet has usable host addresses from 10.0.0.4 through 10.0.0.254. A frequent misunderstanding is to count all theoretical addresses as available; always subtract the reserved addresses. Plan your CIDR ranges with that reservation and operational growth in mind, and avoid overlapping blocks with networks you plan to connect to. CIDR Blocks and IP Allocation means cidr prefix length controls size; aws reserves the first four and the last ip in each subnet, reducing usable addresses.. In practical terms, how cidr defines capacity and the aws reserved addresses you must consider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: CIDR prefix length controls size; AWS reserves the first four and the last IP in each subnet, reducing usable addresses.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CIDR & IP Allocation
CIDR basics
CIDR determines how many addresses a VPC or subnet contains. Smaller prefix values mean more addresses; larger prefix values mean fewer addresses.
Example
10.0.0.0/16 => 65,536 addresses. 10.0.0.0/24 => 256 addresses.
AWS reserved addresses
AWS reserves the first four and the last IP in each subnet. In 10.0.0.0/24, usable hosts start at 10.0.0.4 and end at 10.0.0.254.
Key Takeaway

Always subtract AWS reserved addresses when planning subnet capacity and avoid CIDR overlap with existing networks.

Quick calculator
Prefix /16 → 2^(32-16) = 65,536 addresses
Prefix /24 → 2^(32-24) = 256 addresses
Misconception
Counting theoretical addresses without subtracting AWS-reserved IPs will make you overcommit IP needs. Always factor reservations into design.

screens.title: Public vs Private Subnets
screens.narratorSegment: Public and private subnets are distinguished by routing and intended access. A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway, making instances with public IPs reachable from and able to reach the internet directly. Typical uses include web servers or bastion hosts. A private subnet lacks a direct route to an Internet Gateway; resources there cannot be reached from the internet unless traffic flows through a public subnet or a NAT device. Common use cases include databases and internal application servers. A clear example: place your application front ends in public subnets so they can receive HTTP traffic, and your databases in private subnets to reduce exposure. A frequent mistake is assuming a subnet marked 'public' in name is actually public — the real determinant is whether its route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 entry pointing to an IGW and whether instances have public IPs. Another misconception is that private subnets cannot reach the internet at all; they can, via a NAT Gateway or a proxy hosted in a public subnet, but they remain unreachable from the public internet. Takeaway: classify subnets by routes and IP assignment, not by naming alone.

keyIdea.title: Subnet difference
keyIdea.text: Public subnets route to an IGW and can host internet-facing resources; private subnets do not and are for internal services.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Public vs Private Subnets
Compare roles and routing
Public subnet
Has a route to an Internet Gateway; instances with public IPs can be reached from the internet. Use for web servers and bastion hosts.
Private subnet
No direct route to an Internet Gateway; resources are private. Use for databases and internal services, reachable via NAT or a public proxy.
Key Takeaway

Subnet classification is determined by routes and public IPs, not by labels. Verify route tables and IP assignment.

Scenario
Two-tier app
Place web servers in 10.0.1.0/24 public subnet with IGW route and auto-assigned public IPs. Place DBs in 10.0.2.0/24 private subnet without IGW route.
Misconception
Giving an instance a public IP without the route to an IGW will not enable internet connectivity. Both are required for direct internet access.

screens.title: Internet Gateway (IGW) Role
screens.narratorSegment: The Internet Gateway is the AWS-managed component that allows communication between your VPC and the public internet. It's horizontally scaled and redundant, and it must be attached to your VPC to enable internet-bound traffic. Crucially, the IGW is a target for routes in a route table; adding 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the IGW tells AWS to send all non-local traffic through that gateway. But attaching an IGW to the VPC by itself is not sufficient to make instances reachable: the specific subnet's route table must include the default route to the IGW, and instances must have public IPs. A practical example: attach the IGW then add a route to the public route table; associate that table with a subnet and launch an EC2 with auto-assign public IP turned on. A common error is to attach the IGW but forget to add the default route, or to use a private subnet's route table by mistake. Takeaway: IGW enables internet connectivity only when used together with the correct route table association and public IP configuration on instances. Internet Gateway (IGW) Role means an igw enables internet-bound traffic for subnets that have a route pointing at it; it must be attached and referenced in route tables.. In practical terms, how the igw enables internet-routable traffic for your vpc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: The Internet Gateway is the AWS-managed component that allows communication between your VPC and the public internet. It's horizontally scaled and redundant, and it must be attached to your VPC to enable internet-bound traffic. Crucially, the IGW is a target for routes in a route table; adding 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the IGW tells AWS to send all non-local traffic through that gateway. A practical example: attach the IGW then add a route to the public route table; associate that table with a subnet and launch an EC2 with auto-assign public IP turned on. A common error is to attach the IGW but forget to add the default route, or to use a private subnet's route table by mistake. screens.title: Route Tables & Associations
screens.narratorSegment: Route tables contain the rules that direct traffic from subnets or gateways. Each subnet is associated with exactly one route table; that association determines the effective routing behavior for instances in that subnet. A route table always contains a local route for the VPC CIDR so internal traffic stays within the VPC. For internet access the route table must include a default route such as 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to an Internet Gateway. When you create multiple subnet types, best practice is to create separate route tables: one for public subnets with the IGW route and one for private subnets with no IGW route or with a route to a NAT device. A common troubleshooting step is to check which route table is associated with the subnet. An operation error people make is editing the wrong route table or forgetting to create the default route. Example: create a public route table, add 0.0.0.0/0→igw-xxxx, then explicitly associate it to the public subnet. Takeaway: route table associations, not just the routes themselves, define whether a subnet is public or private. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Launch EC2
EC2 public subnet checklist & user-data
Checklist
  • Subnet associated with route table that routes 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW

screens.title: AWS Reserved Addresses in a Subnet
screens.narratorSegment: When planning subnets, remember AWS reserves addresses you cannot use for instances. Specifically, AWS reserves the first four and the last IP address in every subnet for internal AWS use. For example, in a 10.0.0.0/24 subnet, addresses 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.0.3 are not assignable, and 10.0.0.255 is also reserved. That leaves usable host addresses starting at 10.0.0.4 and ending at 10.0.0.254. This reservation reduces usable capacity compared to the theoretical size of the CIDR block, so design with that in mind. A practical impact is when you plan to run many small instances in a subnet; you must ensure the CIDR block provides enough usable addresses after reservation. A common misunderstanding is to assume all CIDR addresses are available. When calculating IP requirements, subtract the five reserved addresses per subnet from the total. Takeaway: always factor AWS reservations into capacity planning and when subdividing a VPC into multiple subnets across AZs. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › AWS Reserved Addresses
Reserved addresses per subnet
AWS reserves the first four plus the last IP address in each subnet for internal networking functions, reducing the usable host count.
Example calculation
10.0.0.0/24 has 256 theoretical addresses. Subtract five reserved addresses; usable hosts are 251 addresses (from 10.0.0.4 to 10.0.0.254).
Design impact
When splitting a VPC into many /26 or /24 subnets, ensure each subnet’s usable addresses meet your instance and scaling needs after reservation.
Key Takeaway

Remove five addresses per subnet from usable counts when planning capacity.

Misconception
Don't assume you can use the network and broadcast addresses; AWS reserves them internally.

screens.title: High Availability: Subnets and Availability Zones
screens.narratorSegment: High availability in AWS networking comes from distributing resources across multiple Availability Zones. Each subnet lives in a single AZ, so to keep both your public and private tiers resilient you should create at least one public and one private subnet in at least two AZs. For example, place web servers in public subnets in AZ A and AZ B, and databases in private subnets in AZ A and AZ B. This way, if one AZ fails, the other can continue serving traffic. The chapter guidance recommends at least two AZs for high availability of both tiers. A common exam and operational trap is to create multiple subnets but place them all in the same AZ; this yields no AZ-level fault tolerance. When designing, also ensure that your CIDR planning allows for equal-sized subnets per AZ and avoids overlap. Takeaway: align subnet distribution to AZs intentionally so you get fault isolation and continued service during AZ-level failures. Distribute subnets across AZs
Two-AZ pattern
Create public and private subnets in AZ A and AZ B. Place front-end servers in public subnets and databases in private subnets across both AZs.

If one AZ fails, resources in the other AZ continue functioning, preserving availability for users.
Common design mistake
Having all subnets in a single AZ gives no AZ-level fault tolerance even if you have many subnets defined.

Plan one public and one private subnet per AZ and deploy resources cross-AZ for resilience.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn what a Virtual Private Cloud is and why it matters for secure architecture on AWS. A VPC is your private slice of the cloud where you control IP ranges, subnets, route tables, and gateways. Think of it like designing an office building: floors and rooms map to subnets and availability zones, and doors map to gateways and routes. You will see how CIDR notation determines how many addresses you get, how subnets group resources by function and availability zone, and why public and private subnets affect whether resources are reachable from the internet. We will walk through the practical steps to create a VPC, attach an Internet Gateway, set up route tables, and launch an EC2 instance that can serve traffic. Along the way you’ll learn common pitfalls — for example, assigning a route without a public IP will still leave an instance unreachable. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a basic, production-ready VPC with clear reasoning about addressing, isolation, and internet access. Keep the reservation rules and AZ boundaries in mind as you build — they often explain unexpected behavior.

These objectives guide the skills you will practice. First, you will explain the core components and purpose of a VPC: how CIDR ranges, subnets, route tables, and gateways work together to isolate and connect resources. As an example, you'll describe why a 10.0.0.0/16 VPC gives you more addresses than a /24 and why reserved addresses matter. Second, you will design and implement a basic VPC architecture: choose CIDR, create subnets per Availability Zone, attach an Internet Gateway, and configure route tables so specific subnets can reach the internet. Third, you will understand CIDR block allocation and subnetting: you will calculate subnet sizes and avoid overlaps with on-prem networks. Practically, that means picking ranges that leave room for growth. Fourth, you will differentiate public and private subnets and configure an EC2 instance in a public subnet so it can serve or reach the internet, including verifying public IP assignment and correct route table association. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can confirm readiness for architecture decisions and exam-style scenarios.

This page expands the practical skills you will use. You will practice choosing a VPC CIDR that avoids overlap with existing networks so you can peer or build VPNs later. For example, choosing 10.0.0.0/16 gives many addresses, but using 10.0.1.0/24 for a public subnet reserves a small, predictable pool for internet-facing services. You will also associate route tables correctly so that subnets intended to be public have a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway. In practice, a common mistake is creating the route but forgetting to associate it with the subnet, which leaves instances unreachable. You will configure EC2 launch options to auto-assign public IPs or attach Elastic IPs so web servers can be reached. Finally, you will reason about availability zones: each subnet is tied to a single AZ, so high availability requires at least one public and one private subnet in two different AZs. These are the operational skills exam scenarios and production deployments expect you to demonstrate.

A Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, is an isolated virtual network inside AWS where you launch resources under your control. Put simply, it gives you address space, segmentation, and routing the way you would design an on-prem network, but as configurable cloud infrastructure. The VPC's address space is defined with CIDR notation; for example, 10.0.0.0/16 sets the range for the whole VPC. Once defined, you subdivide that space into subnets that live in single Availability Zones. This isolation matters because it separates your workloads from others in the shared AWS environment and lets you enforce precise security and routing rules. A concrete example: you might create a VPC with 10.0.0.0/16, then make a public subnet 10.0.1.0/24 for web servers and a private subnet 10.0.2.0/24 for databases. A common misconception is to assume the VPC alone grants internet access; it does not. An Internet Gateway and the right route configuration are required for internet connectivity. Takeaway: treat the VPC as your network design boundary — plan CIDR, subnets, and AZ mapping before provisioning instances. What is an Amazon VPC? means a vpc is your isolated, configurable network space in aws where you control addressing and connectivity.. In practical terms, an isolated virtual network you design and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing a VPC is a small process with lasting consequences. First, pick a CIDR block for the entire VPC, such as 10.0.0.0/16. This choice defines your total address capacity and must avoid overlap with on-premise or peered VPCs. Second, subdivide the CIDR into subnets aligned to availability zones. For example, split 10.0.0.0/16 into multiple /24 subnets like 10.0.1.0/24 in us-east-1a and 10.0.2.0/24 in us-east-1b. Each subnet belongs to a single AZ; that mapping is the central principle for high availability. Third, classify each subnet as public or private based on whether it will have a route to an Internet Gateway. Public subnets host internet-facing resources; private subnets host internal services like databases. Fourth, plan route tables and associations so intended destinations match the subnet's role. A common error is creating a public route but failing to associate the route table with the subnet, leaving instances with no outbound path. Example: create a public route table with 0.0.0.0/0 -> IGW and associate it to 10.0.1.0/24. Takeaway: design first, then implement, and verify associations and public IP assignments. Designing a VPC: CIDR → Subnets → AZs means choose cidr, carve subnets per az, classify public vs private, and configure routes before launching resources.. In practical terms, a step-by-step design process for a resilient network. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll step through the CLI commands used to build a simple VPC with a public subnet. This walkthrough ties the abstract design to concrete commands and helps you spot the important outputs to record. First, you create the VPC with a CIDR such as 10.0.0.0/16 and note the VpcId. Next, create a subnet in a specific availability zone with a /24 like 10.0.1.0/24 and keep the SubnetId. Then create an Internet Gateway and attach it to the VPC; attach operations must reference both the VpcId and the InternetGatewayId. Create a route table for the VPC, add a route for 0.0.0.0/0 targeting the IGW, and associate the route table with the subnet. A practical mistake to avoid is skipping the associate step or forgetting to enable auto-assign public IP at instance launch. As an example, the aws ec2 create-vpc command returns the VpcId; use that value in subsequent calls. After this sequence you can launch an EC2 into the subnet, ensuring the public IP is assigned. Final takeaway: the sequence matters and recording the returned resource IDs is essential to connect steps.

CIDR notation is the mechanism AWS uses to assign address ranges to VPCs and subnets. It combines a base IP and a prefix length that defines how many bits are fixed, and therefore how many addresses are available. For instance, 10.0.0.0/16 reserves the first 16 bits and yields 2 to the power of 16 addresses, which is 65,536. Subnets use smaller CIDR blocks, like /24, which provides 256 addresses. In AWS, there are additional constraints: the platform reserves the first four and the last IP address in each subnet for internal use. That means in a 10.0.0.0/24 subnet addresses like 10.0.0.0 and 10.0.0.255 are not usable for your instances, plus a few others within the first four. A concrete example: a /24 subnet has usable host addresses from 10.0.0.4 through 10.0.0.254. A frequent misunderstanding is to count all theoretical addresses as available; always subtract the reserved addresses. Plan your CIDR ranges with that reservation and operational growth in mind, and avoid overlapping blocks with networks you plan to connect to. CIDR Blocks and IP Allocation means cidr prefix length controls size; aws reserves the first four and the last ip in each subnet, reducing usable addresses.. Public and private subnets are distinguished by routing and intended access. A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway, making instances with public IPs reachable from and able to reach the internet directly. Typical uses include web servers or bastion hosts. A private subnet lacks a direct route to an Internet Gateway; resources there cannot be reached from the internet unless traffic flows through a public subnet or a NAT device. Common use cases include databases and internal application servers. A clear example: place your application front ends in public subnets so they can receive HTTP traffic, and your databases in private subnets to reduce exposure. A frequent mistake is assuming a subnet marked 'public' in name is actually public — the real determinant is whether its route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 entry pointing to an IGW and whether instances have public IPs. Another misconception is that private subnets cannot reach the internet at all; they can, via a NAT Gateway or a proxy hosted in a public subnet, but they remain unreachable from the public internet. Takeaway: classify subnets by routes and IP assignment, not by naming alone.

The Internet Gateway is the AWS-managed component that allows communication between your VPC and the public internet. It's horizontally scaled and redundant, and it must be attached to your VPC to enable internet-bound traffic. Crucially, the IGW is a target for routes in a route table; adding 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the IGW tells AWS to send all non-local traffic through that gateway. But attaching an IGW to the VPC by itself is not sufficient to make instances reachable: the specific subnet's route table must include the default route to the IGW, and instances must have public IPs. A practical example: attach the IGW then add a route to the public route table; associate that table with a subnet and launch an EC2 with auto-assign public IP turned on. A common error is to attach the IGW but forget to add the default route, or to use a private subnet's route table by mistake. Takeaway: IGW enables internet connectivity only when used together with the correct route table association and public IP configuration on instances. Route tables contain the rules that direct traffic from subnets or gateways. Each subnet is associated with exactly one route table; that association determines the effective routing behavior for instances in that subnet. A route table always contains a local route for the VPC CIDR so internal traffic stays within the VPC. For internet access the route table must include a default route such as 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to an Internet Gateway. When you create multiple subnet types, best practice is to create separate route tables: one for public subnets with the IGW route and one for private subnets with no IGW route or with a route to a NAT device. A common troubleshooting step is to check which route table is associated with the subnet. An operation error people make is editing the wrong route table or forgetting to create the default route. Example: create a public route table, add 0.0.0.0/0→igw-xxxx, then explicitly associate it to the public subnet. Takeaway: route table associations, not just the routes themselves, define whether a subnet is public or private. When planning subnets, remember AWS reserves addresses you cannot use for instances. Specifically, AWS reserves the first four and the last IP address in every subnet for internal AWS use. For example, in a 10.0.0.0/24 subnet, addresses 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.0.3 are not assignable, and 10.0.0.255 is also reserved. That leaves usable host addresses starting at 10.0.0.4 and ending at 10.0.0.254. This reservation reduces usable capacity compared to the theoretical size of the CIDR block, so design with that in mind. A practical impact is when you plan to run many small instances in a subnet; you must ensure the CIDR block provides enough usable addresses after reservation. A common misunderstanding is to assume all CIDR addresses are available. When calculating IP requirements, subtract the five reserved addresses per subnet from the total. Takeaway: always factor AWS reservations into capacity planning and when subdividing a VPC into multiple subnets across AZs. High availability in AWS networking comes from distributing resources across multiple Availability Zones. Each subnet lives in a single AZ, so to keep both your public and private tiers resilient you should create at least one public and one private subnet in at least two AZs. For example, place web servers in public subnets in AZ A and AZ B, and databases in private subnets in AZ A and AZ B. This way, if one AZ fails, the other can continue serving traffic. The chapter guidance recommends at least two AZs for high availability of both tiers. A common exam and operational trap is to create multiple subnets but place them all in the same AZ; this yields no AZ-level fault tolerance. When designing, also ensure that your CIDR planning allows for equal-sized subnets per AZ and avoids overlap. Takeaway: align subnet distribution to AZs intentionally so you get fault isolation and continued service during AZ-level failures. Let's summarize the most important concepts you should retain. First, a VPC is your isolated network boundary in AWS: you define its CIDR, carve subnets, and control routing and gateways. Second, CIDR and AWS reservations matter when planning capacity: choose prefixes that provide enough usable IPs after subtracting the first four and last address that AWS reserves per subnet. Third, public versus private subnets are defined by routes and public IP assignment: a subnet is public only if its route table sends default traffic to an Internet Gateway and instances have public IPs. As you design and implement, follow the checklist: plan CIDR, split subnets by AZ, attach IGW for public subnets, configure route tables and associations correctly, and ensure instances have public IPs when they need internet reachability. Keep these ideas in mind and you’ll avoid the most common misconfigurations.
